title: Hand tools, cutting tools and sharp waste
audience: Garden clean-up workers who use secateurs, loppers, saws, rakes, forks and shovels, and who collect thorny, glass and other sharp debris.
learningOutcomes: Inspect hand and cutting tools before use and remove defective tools from service.
Use cutting tools with control of hand position, cut direction and body position.
Separate and package thorns, glass, needles and other sharp waste without hand-sorting mixed heaps.
Store cutting tools safely during and after the job.

instruction.heading: Why hand tools cause garden injuries
instruction.body: Hand tools look simple, and that is why they cause so many cuts and puncture wounds in garden work. A blade that has been left unsharpened slips rather than cuts, so the worker pushes harder and loses control. A rake with a bent tine catches on a root and throws the user off balance. A loppers handle with a split grip pinches a finger. Sharp waste adds another layer. Broken glass, thorny stems, rusty wire and discarded needles can be hidden in leaves, mulch and soil. The safe approach is to inspect the tool before use, control the cut, and keep your hands away from anything you have not yet seen clearly.

instruction.heading: Inspecting and selecting tools
instruction.body: Before each shift, inspect the tools you will use. Check that blades are sharp and free of nicks, that the pivot or bolt is tight, and that the spring on secateurs opens fully. Check that saw teeth are intact and the blade is not bent, and that the handle is firm and free of cracks or splinters. Replace or remove from service any tool with a loose head, a cracked handle, a damaged guard or a blade that cannot be sharpened safely. Select the tool for the job. Use secateurs for stems within their rated diameter and loppers for thicker stems. Use a hand saw for material that a pruner cannot cut cleanly. Do not force a tool beyond its capacity. Do not use a hand tool as a lever on a pallet, a branch under load or a stone. Keep sheaths, scabbards and guards in place when tools are not in use.

instruction.heading: Cutting with control
instruction.body: Plan each cut before you make it. Identify where the cut will land and where the stem or branch will fall, and keep your feet and other people's feet out of that line. Use a stable stance, keep your free hand clear of the cutting line, and cut away from your body. When cutting a stem under tension, expect it to spring or split. Support heavy material before the final cut. Use two hands on loppers and keep the handle grip clean and dry. Do not reach over or through dense growth to cut. Move the stems you are cutting toward you, or move your position. If a stem is caught in a fence, a wire or a service, stop and assess before continuing. Clean and oil blades at the end of the job, and store tools with the blades protected and the handles dry.

instruction.heading: Sharp waste and safe packaging
instruction.body: Garden debris often contains sharp hazards. Thorny stems, broken glass and metal, rusted wire and needles all require care. Do not hand-sort a mixed heap. Use a rake, fork or shovel to move the pile, and look before you reach. If a needle or unknown sharp object is found, stop, keep others away, and do not pick it up by hand. Follow the site procedure for needles and report the find to the supervisor. Place broken glass and sharp metal in a rigid, labelled, puncture-resistant container, and keep thorny plant waste separate in a bag or bin that resists puncture. Do not overfill containers. Seal them and mark them so that the next person knows what they contain. Sharp waste that is not clean green waste goes to the stream that the business has confirmed for it, which is covered in the waste separation lesson.

instruction.heading: Verification and escalation
instruction.body: A supervisor should observe the inspection, the cutting technique and the packaging. A competent worker can show that they inspected their secateurs, select the right tool for a given stem, explain where a falling branch will land and identify the packaging for sharp waste. Stop and report any tool that cracks, slips or behaves unexpectedly, any cut that causes a deep wound, any needle find, and any sharp waste that cannot be contained. Injuries must be treated under the business's first-aid procedure and recorded, even when they seem minor.

procedure: Inspect each hand tool and saw before use for sharpness, tightness, cracks, guards and handle condition.
Remove any defective tool from service, tag it and tell the supervisor.
Select the correct tool for each stem size and material, and avoid forcing tools beyond their capacity.
Plan each cut, clear the fall zone and keep your free hand out of the cutting line.
Move loose debris with a rake or fork, and look before reaching into any pile.
Place sharp waste in a rigid, labelled, puncture-resistant container, and place thorny green waste in a puncture-resistant bag.
Stop and report any needle or unknown sharp object without touching it.
Clean, dry and store tools with their guards in place at the end of the job, and record any defective tool.

workedExamples.situation: A crew member is cutting a rose cane with secateurs when the spring breaks and the blade slips toward the hand that is holding the stem.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the worker do with the tool, and what was the missed control?
workedExamples.reasoning: The worker should stop, remove the secateurs from service, tag them as defective and report the failure. The missed control was the pre-use inspection, which should have checked the spring and the blade. The worker should also have kept the free hand clear of the cutting line. Treat any cut as an injury under the first-aid procedure and record it.

workedExamples.situation: A pile of cut stems and mulch contains broken glass and a single used needle near the bottom.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How do you clear the pile safely?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop hand-sorting. Keep others back from the pile. Do not pick up the needle. Move the top layer with a rake or fork, and look at each layer before reaching in. Report the needle to the supervisor and follow the site procedure. Place the glass in a rigid labelled container and the thorny stems in a puncture-resistant bag.

equipmentAndPpe: Cut-resistant gloves suitable for pruning and handling thorny material
Eye protection for cutting and for debris clearing
Rigid, labelled puncture-resistant container for glass and sharp metal
Puncture-resistant bag or bin for thorny green waste
Rake, fork and shovel for moving debris without hand contact

commonErrors.error: Using a blade that is blunt or has a loose pivot, then forcing the cut.
commonErrors.prevention: Inspect and sharpen before use. Remove any defective tool and report it.

commonErrors.error: Holding the stem with the free hand in the cutting line.
commonErrors.prevention: Plan the cut and keep the free hand clear. Move the stem or your position instead of reaching into the line.

commonErrors.error: Hand-sorting a mixed pile of debris to find the rubbish.
commonErrors.prevention: Move the pile with a rake or fork and look before reaching. Report needles and unknown sharps.

commonErrors.error: Throwing broken glass into a green-waste bag because it is only a small piece.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a rigid, labelled, puncture-resistant container for glass and keep it out of green waste.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Hand-tool and cutting-tool use falls under the model WHS framework's general duty to manage risk, to the level that is reasonably practicable.

Cutting work at height, or in or near trees, may need a licence or council permit, and it is excluded from this business. Do not use hand or powered cutting tools to work on a tree above a set height or near a power line.
Needles and other sharp waste found on a site must be handled under the site procedure, and the rules for their disposal vary by state, territory and council.

qualityStandard: Every hand and cutting tool used on the job has been inspected before use and any defect has been removed from service.
Cuts are planned and controlled, and the fall zone is clear of people.
Sharp waste is contained in labelled, puncture-resistant containers and is not hand-sorted.
No needle or unknown sharp object has been picked up by hand.
documentationEvidence: Tool inspection record for the job, including tools removed from service and the reason.
Record of sharp waste containers, their contents and their destination.
Injury or near-miss record for any cut, puncture or slip, with first-aid treatment recorded.
summary: Inspect every hand tool before use and remove defective tools from service.
Plan each cut, keep the free hand clear and cut away from the body.
Do not hand-sort mixed debris. Move it with tools and report needles.
Package sharp waste in rigid, labelled, puncture-resistant containers.

knowledgeChecks.question: A pair of secateurs has a spring that will not open fully. What is the correct action?
options: Remove them from service, tag them and report the defect.
Use them anyway, since the blade still cuts.
Spray lubricant on the spring and continue for the rest of the day.

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker finds a used needle at the bottom of a pile of debris. What should they do?
options: Pick it up with gloves and place it in the green-waste bin, since the gloves protect the hands fully.
Stop, keep others back, do not pick up the needle, and report it under the site procedure.
Move it to one side with a bare hand and continue sorting the pile without any further delay today.

knowledgeChecks.question: Where should broken glass from a garden clean-up be placed?
options: In a green-waste bag, since it is only a small amount and the bag is strong.
Under the mulch, so that it is not visible to the client and the bed looks tidy.
In a puncture-resistant, labelled, rigid container kept separate from green waste.

knowledgeChecks.question: What should be checked on secateurs before each shift, according to the lesson?
options: Nothing, once they were used before
